title: The Iliad: The Wrath of Achilles
author: Homer
intro: A história de um guerreiro cuja ira causa sofrimento a todos, e de um final surpreendente em que dois inimigos choram juntos.

B2.text: The Iliad tells the story of a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War. Achilles is the best Greek warrior, but he becomes angry with King Agamemnon, who takes away a woman that Achilles had received as a prize. Achilles refuses to fight, and without him the Greeks begin to lose. Then his close friend Patroclus goes into battle wearing Achilles's armour, and Hector, the Trojan prince, kills him. Achilles's anger turns against Hector. He returns to the war and kills him. At the end, Hector's father, King Priam, secretly visits Achilles to ask for his son's body, and Achilles, moved, agrees.

C1.text: The Iliad opens with a single word, 'wrath', and the poem never ceases to examine its consequences. Slighted by Agamemnon, who seizes his war prize, Achilles withdraws from battle, and his absence exacts a heavy toll on the Greeks. Only the death of his companion Patroclus, killed by Hector while wearing Achilles's armour, drags him back into the fighting, now motivated not by honour but by grief and vengeance. Having slain Hector, he abuses the corpse. The poem, however, refuses to end in triumph: when Priam risks his life to beg for his son's body, the two enemies weep together, and a fragile compassion briefly overcomes the logic of war.

C2.text: What distinguishes the Iliad from a mere celebration of martial prowess is its unflinching attention to loss. Achilles's quarrel with Agamemnon is nominally about honour, yet the poem gradually reveals honour to be an insufficient consolation for mortality. Offered every reparation, Achilles first refuses, only to be undone by Patroclus's death, after which his rage becomes self-consuming. The epic's closing movement, in which Achilles and Priam share a fleeting recognition of their common vulnerability, does not resolve the war; Troy's fall lies beyond the poem's end. Instead, it suggests that the deepest response to suffering is not glory but the capacity to acknowledge another's grief.
